No official SWISS national net (take-home) monthly median income figure could be obtained from the Federal Statistical Office's published outputs. This is a PUBLICATION gap, not a data gap and not a fetch outage: the Swiss Earnings Structure Survey (Lohnstrukturerhebung, LSE) demonstrably DOES collect net wage data - a cantonal statistical office quotes national net wage distribution thresholds derived from it (see 020_net_monthly_income.json) - but every BFS-published LSE table reached in this research is a GROSS table, and no net median is exposed. Switzerland's structural context makes this gap harder to fill elsewhere too: federal, cantonal and municipal income taxes all apply, so there is no single national net figure to find even in principle, and any net number must be canton-specific. No net figure was invented to fill the gap.

sources.notes: ETH Zurich replaced its two-tier fee structure in Autumn Semester 2025 with a Simple / Threefold structure covering both tuition and semester fees combined. A third-country national Bachelor student without a qualifying EU/EFTA permit status pays the threefold fee of CHF 2,190 per semester, so CHF 4,380 for a standard two-semester year. The page is explicit that a permit carrying only 'right to gainful employment up to 15 hrs/week' is NOT sufficient for the simple fee, which matters because that is exactly the status most students hold. Reallocation to the simple group must be requested before enrolment and is not possible during studies. ETH is the federal institute, so this is also the cheapest-case official tuition benchmark for a highly selective public university, not a general Swiss average. UZH (University of Zurich) publishes a different structure — CHF 720 per semester plus a CHF 500 surcharge for foreign students at Bachelor level plus CHF 59 mandatory semester contributions, from https://www.uzh.ch/en/studies/application/fees.html — recorded as a second university in file 006.

sources.notes: Permanent residence in Switzerland is the C permit (Niederlassungsbewilligung), described by SEM as granted 'after five or ten years' residence in Switzerland'. The five-year figure is verified for the EU-15 and EFTA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway) list printed on the page. The ten-year figure applies to other groups, but I could not fetch the federal page that states the ten-year rule for third-country nationals specifically: sem.admin.ch/sem/en/home/themen/aufenthalt/nicht_eu_efta/ausweis_c.html returned 404 and the English naturalisation page returned 404, and the SEM free-movement FAQ I did fetch only clarifies the EU/EFTA side ('nationals from states other than those mentioned above are granted a settlement permit after a regular period of ten years', referring to remaining EU member states, not third countries). So the ten-year third-country minimum is reported as UNAVAILABLE within this file rather than asserted. Two further qualifications from the same federal source set: the free-movement agreement does not cover permanent residence, and the SEM determines the earliest date from which cantonal authorities may grant the permit, so a C permit is not automatic on the fifth anniversary. Importantly for scholarship applicants, time on a study permit is residence, but the C permit itself is residence-based, not study-based: no Swiss route was found that converts a completed degree into permanent residence directly.
sources.publisher: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM), Federal Department of Justice and Police
sources.title: permanent_residence evidence

sources.notes: Canton Zurich is the cantonal authority that issues the permits it describes, so this is an official regional source for the rule rather than a university summary. Key points: the permission is a cantonal Bewilligung for Nebenbeschäftigung (part-time employment), applied for by the employer, not the student; the 15-hour weekly cap applies outside school holidays, so term-time part-time work is capped but holiday work is not capped on this page; employment may not begin earlier than six months after the start of the programme; three cumulative conditions apply (school confirms the job fits within the programme, the job must not delay graduation, and the 15-hour term-time cap). This is the 'percentage FTE' rule expressed in hours: 15 hours per week against a nominal full-time week, i.e. roughly a 37.5% FTE in term time. For comparison, the SEM free-movement FAQ fetched from the federal source confirms the equivalent EU/EFTA figure: 'Students are issued this permit for one year and are granted yearly renewals until the completion of their studies, if they continue to fulfil the respective conditions' and notes that the free-movement agreement does not cover permanent residence. Post-study: a six-month short-stay permit for job search is available on graduation, and a six-month Kurzaufenthaltsbewilligung after a completed degree is confirmed above. Separately, the Canton Zurich page states that graduates of a Swiss higher-education institution may be admitted to work under a cantonal permit where the field has a shortage of labour ('In Frage kommen nur Bereiche, in denen nicht bereits ein genügendes Angebot an Arbeitskräften besteht'), which is a labour-shortage test rather than an automatic right. No claim is made about a national maximum working percentage because no federal page stating one was fetchable; the figures above are cantonal.
